subject: Banking
title: Can We Prevent the Next Failure?
description: A micro-lesson that makes Can We Prevent the Next Failure? usable.

hook.text: After every bank failure, politicians say 'never again.' After every boom, they weaken the rules they wrote.

buildup.text: Glass-Steagall lasted 66 years. Dodd-Frank was weakened within 8.

discovery.text: Better regulation helps but can't eliminate risk. Banking requires maturity transformation, which is inherently fragile.

twist.text: The banking industry spends $700 million annually lobbying Congress. The biggest spenders are the biggest banks.

climax.text: Banking failures can be reduced but not eliminated. The system is designed to take risks.

punchline.text: $700 million in lobbying. The cycle of crisis and reform will never end.

quiz.question: How much does the banking industry spend on lobbying annually?

details.summary: Despite decades of regulation, stress testing, and higher capital requirements since 2008, the 2023 bank failures showed that new risks keep emerging. The question is whether the banking system can ever be made truly failure-proof.
details.whyItMatters: If bank failures are inevitable despite regulation, the focus shifts to building systems that can absorb failures without systemic damage. Understanding these limits helps set realistic expectations for financial stability.
takeaways: Post-2008 regulations significantly increased bank capital and oversight
The 2023 failures revealed risks from interest rate exposure not caught by stress tests
Complete prevention is likely impossible so containment matters more

faq.question: Why do banks keep failing despite better regulation?
faq.answer: Each crisis originates from risks that previous regulations did not anticipate. The 2008 crisis came from securitization, while 2023 failures came from interest rate risk. Regulations address past problems while future risks take new and unexpected forms.

faq.question: What approach works better than trying to prevent all failures?
faq.answer: Building a system that can absorb individual bank failures without contagion is more realistic. This means adequate deposit insurance, effective resolution mechanisms, and reducing interconnections that allow one failure to cascade across the system.
